marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q001.takeaway: Zona orbicularis is the circular capsular fiber ring around the femoral neck.
marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q001.displayText:
Zona orbicularis is the circular capsular fiber ring around the femoral neck.

Zona orbicularis is related to the neck of femur. It consists of circular fibres of the capsule of the hip joint.

The hip capsule has two sets of fibres: circular fibres (zona orbicularis), which are internal and form a collar around the femoral neck and blend with pubofemoral and ischiofemoral ligaments; and longitudinal fibres, which are external, are numerous anterosuperiorly and are joined by the iliofemoral ligament.
emphasis: Zona orbicularis is the circular capsular fiber ring around the femoral neck

rationales.a: The tibial tuberosity is an attachment on the proximal tibia and is unrelated to the hip capsule.
rationales.c: The anatomical neck is a proximal humeral landmark; zona orbicularis encircles the femoral neck.
rationales.d: The ankle joint is far distal from the hip capsule fibers forming zona orbicularis.

marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q002.takeaway: The transverse acetabular ligament bridges the acetabular notch and continues with the acetabular labrum; the ligament itself is not cartilage.
marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q002.displayText:
The transverse acetabular ligament bridges the acetabular notch and continues with the acetabular labrum; the ligament itself is not cartilage.

The false statement is that the transverse acetabular ligament contains cartilage cells. It crosses the acetabular notch and continues peripherally with the labrum.

Ligaments of the hip joint: iliofemoral ligament is the strongest; pubofemoral ligament is triangular; some ischiofemoral fibres fuse with zona orbicularis and inferior fibres attach to the posterior circumference of the femoral neck; the transverse acetabular ligament forms a foramen allowing vessels and nerves to enter the joint; the ligament of the head of femur has its apex attached to the fovea and base to the margins of the acetabular notch.

Source note: iliocapsularis lies immediately deep to the iliopsoas tendon and above the anterior hip capsule. Its function is unclear and is thought to taut the hip capsule to prevent impingement during hip flexion.
emphasis: The transverse acetabular ligament bridges the acetabular notch and continues with the acetabular labrum; the ligament itself is not cartilage

rationales.a: The iliofemoral ligament is the strongest hip ligament, so this statement is true.
rationales.c: Ischiofemoral fibers can blend with the circular zona orbicularis, as the source describes.
rationales.d: The pubofemoral ligament is triangular, so this statement is true.

marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q003.takeaway: The iliofemoral ligament is the strongest hip ligament and checks hyperextension.
marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q003.displayText:
The iliofemoral ligament is the strongest hip ligament and checks hyperextension.

The iliofemoral ligament resists hyperextension of the hip joint and is therefore likely to be injured.

The iliofemoral ligament (ligament of Bigelow) is the strongest ligament of the hip. It is an inverted-Y-shaped ligament; its apex is attached between the anterior inferior iliac spine and acetabular margin and its base attaches to the intertrochanteric line. It prevents hyperextension.
emphasis: The iliofemoral ligament is the strongest hip ligament and checks hyperextension

rationales.a: The pubofemoral ligament chiefly limits excessive abduction and extension but is not the principal strong check on hyperextension.
rationales.b: The ischiofemoral ligament is posterior and limits internal rotation/extension; the key anterior restraint to hyperextension is iliofemoral.
rationales.d: The ligament of the femoral head carries a small vessel and is not the principal capsular restraint to hyperextension.

marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q004.takeaway: A partially flexed, abducted hip increases capsular capacity and is the position of greatest comfort with effusion.
marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q004.displayText:
A partially flexed, abducted hip increases capsular capacity and is the position of greatest comfort with effusion.

A patient with hip-joint effusion has least pain in the flexed and abducted position. Joint capacity is maximal with the hip partially flexed and abducted, making this the position of greatest comfort.
emphasis: A partially flexed, abducted hip increases capsular capacity and is the position of greatest comfort with effusion

rationales.a: Full flexion with adduction is not the resting position that maximizes joint capacity in an effusion.
rationales.b: Extension and abduction tighten the capsule and do not maximize hip-joint capacity.
rationales.d: Extension with adduction is a tense position rather than the comfortable partially flexed, abducted posture.

marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q005.takeaway: The foveal artery in the ligament of the femoral head usually comes from the acetabular branch of the obturator artery.
marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q005.displayText:
The foveal artery in the ligament of the femoral head usually comes from the acetabular branch of the obturator artery.

The marked structure is the ligament of the head of femur. The artery passing through it is the foveal artery/artery of the ligament of the head of femur, derived from the acetabular branch of the obturator artery.

The femoral head also receives blood from the trochanteric arterial ring formed by medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries with minor contributions from superior and inferior gluteal vessels.
emphasis: The foveal artery in the ligament of the femoral head usually comes from the acetabular branch of the obturator artery

rationales.a: Medial circumflex femoral retinacular branches provide the major adult head supply but do not pass through the ligament of the head.
rationales.b: The lateral circumflex contributes to circumflex anastomoses but is not the source of the foveal artery described.
rationales.d: Profunda femoris gives circumflex/perforating branches, but the artery traversing the ligament is the obturator-derived acetabular branch.

marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q006.takeaway: Tibial plateau labels 1, 5 and 6 mark the ACL, PCL and anterior/posterior horns of the medial meniscus, respectively.
marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q006.displayText:
Tibial plateau labels 1, 5 and 6 mark the ACL, PCL and anterior/posterior horns of the medial meniscus, respectively.

The structures attached to areas 1, 5 and 6 are, respectively, the anterior cruciate ligament, posterior cruciate ligament, and the anterior and posterior horns of the medial meniscus.

The source mnemonic for attachments from anterior to posterior is 'Medial College Ludhiana Ludhiana Medical College': medial meniscus (anterior horn), cruciate ligament (anterior), lateral meniscus (anterior horn), lateral meniscus (posterior horn), medial meniscus (posterior horn), cruciate ligament (posterior).
emphasis: Tibial plateau labels 1, 5 and 6 mark the ACL, PCL and anterior/posterior horns of the medial meniscus, respectively

rationales.b: Option B assigns medial meniscal horns to labels 1 and 5, whereas the source figure places the ACL and PCL there.
rationales.c: Option C substitutes lateral-meniscus horns for the medial-meniscus horns at label 6.
rationales.d: Option D assigns meniscal horns to the first two labels instead of the ACL and PCL shown in the source figure.

marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q007.takeaway: The classic unhappy triad is ACL, tibial collateral (MCL) and medial meniscus injury; the keyed option contains the ACL and medial meniscus but omits MCL.
marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q007.displayText:
The classic unhappy triad is ACL, tibial collateral (MCL) and medial meniscus injury; the keyed option contains the ACL and medial meniscus but omits MCL.

The unhappy triad of the knee involves the medial meniscus, anterior cruciate ligament and tibial collateral ligament. Among the answer choices, anterior cruciate ligament and medial meniscus are therefore the matching components.
emphasis: The classic unhappy triad is ACL, tibial collateral (MCL) and medial meniscus injury; the keyed option contains the ACL and medial meniscus but omits MCL

rationales.a: This pair names both menisci but omits the ACL and tibial collateral ligament, which are components of the classic triad.
rationales.b: PCL and lateral meniscus are not the classic structures in the valgus-impact unhappy triad.
rationales.d: Lateral meniscus horns are not the classic combination; the source-keyed choice is the closest listed pair but is incomplete because MCL is absent.

audit.tablesAndFigures: Retained by unchanged native structuredExplanation and source figure metadata.
audit.medicalReviewNote: The traditional unhappy triad includes ACL, tibial collateral ligament, and medial meniscus; no option gives all three. The printed key selects the closest pair (ACL and medial meniscus), which the source explanation also identifies as only the matching components. Preserve key pending question review.

marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q008.takeaway: Coronary ligaments are meniscotibial attachments that tether the menisci to the tibial plateau.
marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q008.displayText:
Coronary ligaments are meniscotibial attachments that tether the menisci to the tibial plateau.

Coronary ligaments are also known as meniscotibial ligaments and refer to the tibial attachment of the medial meniscus.

The medial meniscus is almost semicircular. Its anterior horn attaches to the anterior tibial intercondylar area in front of the anterior cruciate ligament; the posterior horn fixes to the posterior tibial intercondylar area between the attachments of the lateral meniscus and posterior cruciate ligament. These attachments make the medial meniscus relatively fixed and less mobile than the lateral meniscus.
emphasis: Coronary ligaments are meniscotibial attachments that tether the menisci to the tibial plateau

rationales.a: Meniscofemoral ligaments connect the lateral meniscus to the femur near the PCL, not the tibia.
rationales.b: The posterior meniscofemoral ligament is a femoral attachment of the lateral meniscus, not a coronary ligament.
rationales.c: The oblique popliteal ligament reinforces the posterior knee capsule and is not the meniscotibial attachment.

marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q009.takeaway: The lateral meniscus is more mobile than the relatively fixed medial meniscus, so saying its movement is more restricted is false.
marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q009.displayText:
The lateral meniscus is more mobile than the relatively fixed medial meniscus, so saying its movement is more restricted is false.

The false statement is that movement of the lateral meniscus is restricted compared with the medial meniscus. In fact, the medial meniscus is relatively fixed and moves less; the lateral meniscus is more mobile.

Peripheral meniscal zones are vascularized by capillary loops while inner regions are less vascular, so peripheral tears heal better. The suprapatellar bursa is the superior extension of the knee-joint cavity and lies between the femur and suprapatellar part of quadriceps femoris.
emphasis: The lateral meniscus is more mobile than the relatively fixed medial meniscus, so saying its movement is more restricted is false

rationales.a: The lateral meniscus covers a larger part of the tibial articular surface than the medial meniscus; this statement is true.
rationales.c: Peripheral meniscal regions have better vascular supply, so their tears generally heal better than central tears.
rationales.d: The suprapatellar bursa communicates with and is an extension of the knee-joint cavity.

marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q010.takeaway: In open-chain extension, the tibia medially rotates on the femur to lock the knee; equivalently, the femur rotates laterally on a fixed tibia.
marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q010.displayText:
In open-chain extension, the tibia medially rotates on the femur to lock the knee; equivalently, the femur rotates laterally on a fixed tibia.

Locking of the knee is medial rotation of the femur on the tibia during the later stages of extension.

When standing, the knee locks to reduce muscular work needed to maintain posture; the source states vastus medialis is responsible for locking. Unlocking is lateral rotation of the femur on the tibia at the beginning of flexion and is produced by popliteus.
emphasis: In open-chain extension, the tibia medially rotates on the femur to lock the knee; equivalently, the femur rotates laterally on a fixed tibia

rationales.a: In closed-chain extension the femur medially rotates on the tibia; lateral femoral rotation is the opposite direction of the screw-home lock.
rationales.b: Flexion begins with unlocking, the opposite rotational direction from terminal extension locking.
rationales.c: Lateral rotation during flexion describes an unlocking motion rather than the terminal extension lock.

marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q011.takeaway: Clergyman's knee is infrapatellar bursitis; housemaid's knee is prepatellar bursitis.
marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q011.displayText:
Clergyman's knee is infrapatellar bursitis; housemaid's knee is prepatellar bursitis.

Clergyman's knee and housemaid's knee result from inflammation of the infrapatellar bursa and prepatellar bursa respectively.

The source lists major lower-limb bursitides: prepatellar bursitis (housemaid's knee), infrapatellar bursitis (clergyman's knee), and trochanteric bursitis above the hip abductor.
emphasis: Clergyman's knee is infrapatellar bursitis; housemaid's knee is prepatellar bursitis

rationales.a: This reverses the named associations: prepatellar is housemaid's knee and infrapatellar is clergyman's knee.
rationales.b: The subcutaneous and deep infrapatellar bursae are both near the patellar tendon, not the clergyman/housemaid pair in the stated order.
rationales.d: The suprapatellar bursa communicates with the knee joint and is not the clergyman/housemaid pair.

marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q012.takeaway: Ligamentum mucosum is an infrapatellar synovial plica within the knee joint.
marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q012.displayText:
Ligamentum mucosum is an infrapatellar synovial plica within the knee joint.

Ligamentum mucosum is related to the knee joint and is a plica at the intercondylar notch.

Plicae are embryological remnants of synovial folds. Major knee plicae listed are ligamentum mucosum at the intercondylar notch, suprapatellar plica in the suprapatellar space, and medial plica extending from the infrapatellar fat pad to the medial wall of the knee.

Plica syndrome is a painful knee condition due to thickened/inflamed synovial folds, most commonly involving the medial plica.
emphasis: Ligamentum mucosum is an infrapatellar synovial plica within the knee joint

rationales.a: The temporomandibular joint is not the location of ligamentum mucosum.
rationales.b: The hip joint has its own capsule and ligaments; the mucosal ligament/plica described is in the knee.
rationales.c: The shoulder joint is anatomically unrelated to this knee synovial fold.

marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q013.takeaway: Inversion sprains most often injure the anterior talofibular ligament, especially with plantarflexion.
marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q013.displayText:
Inversion sprains most often injure the anterior talofibular ligament, especially with plantarflexion.

The anterior talofibular ligament is most commonly injured in inversion sprains.

Lateral ankle ligaments likely to be injured with inversion include anterior talofibular ligament (most common), posterior talofibular ligament and calcaneofibular ligament. Medial ligaments more likely injured with eversion include the deltoid (medial collateral) ligament and spring (calcaneonavicular) ligament.
emphasis: Inversion sprains most often injure the anterior talofibular ligament, especially with plantarflexion

rationales.a: The deltoid ligament is medial and is more vulnerable with eversion rather than inversion.
rationales.c: The spring ligament supports the talar head and medial arch, not the lateral ankle ligament injured in inversion.
rationales.d: The posterior talofibular ligament is part of the lateral complex but is less commonly injured than ATFL.

marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q014.takeaway: The superficial deltoid fibers attach to the navicular, talus and calcaneus; the fibula is lateral and is not a deltoid attachment.
marrow__ANAT_CH55_Q014.displayText:
The superficial deltoid fibers attach to the navicular, talus and calcaneus; the fibula is lateral and is not a deltoid attachment.

The superficial part of the deltoid ligament is attached to all listed bones except the fibula.

The deltoid/medial collateral ligament is a strong triangular band attached to the apex and anterior/posterior borders of the medial malleolus. The source describes two layers. Superficial layer: tibionavicular fibres anteriorly, tibiocalcaneal fibres in the middle, and superficial posterior tibiotalar fibres posteriorly. Deep layer: anterior tibiotalar fibres, tibiocalcaneal fibres in the middle, and deep posterior tibiotalar fibres posteriorly.
emphasis: The superficial deltoid fibers attach to the navicular, talus and calcaneus; the fibula is lateral and is not a deltoid attachment

rationales.a: Tibionavicular fibers attach to the navicular as part of the superficial deltoid layer.
rationales.b: Tibiotalar fibers attach the deltoid ligament to the talus.
rationales.c: Tibiocalcaneal fibers attach to the calcaneus.
